newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada court clears way for Voisey's Bay projects.
newsitem.headline: Canada court clears way for Voisey's Bay projects.

text.p: Canada's massive Voisey's Bay nickel project cleared a major hurdle on Friday after a Canadian court rejected a bid by two native groups to stop construction projects at the site.

After the court ruling, the Newfoundland government said that Inco Ltd., the western world's biggest nickel producer, would not have to wait long for permits to build an airstrip and road at Voisey's Bay in a remote part of Labrador.

Voisey's Bay, one of the world's biggest nickel-copper-cobalt deposits, is set to start producing concentrate in late 1999 and refined nickel by late 2000. Annual output is forecast at 270 million pounds of nickel when the mine reaches full production in 2001.
Analysts said the court ruling was positive for Inco, but that the Toronto-based company faced other challenges that might delay the project's planned start-up in late 1999.
Newfoundland's Supreme Court on Friday dismissed an application by the Labrador Inuit Association and Innu Nation to block the construction projects.
The native groups argued that the projects were production work and should not be approved by the Newfoundland government until the completion of a broader environmental review of Voisey's Bay.
Inco maintained the airstrip and road were intended only for exploration of the site and Newfoundland Justice Raymond Halley agreed.
"The works are necessary to support the ongoing exploratory activity," Halley said in a written decision.
The Labrador Inuit Association said it was disappointed by the decision and was considering an appeal.
"What the judge has done is say it's okay for the province to issue the permits. So we're waiting for the permits," Inco spokesman David Allen said in a telephone interview.
Sean Kelly, a spokesman for Newfoundland's Department of Environment and Labor, said permits for the airstrip and road should be granted soon.
Meanwhile, analysts said other factors could upset Inco's timetable.
A source of electricity for the nickel smelter has not been decided and negotiations between the Newfoundland government and aboriginal groups to resolve land claims at Voisey's Bay drag on.
"It (the court ruling) is certainly is a positive move for Inco, but I don't think this will alleviate all the concerns about the planning of the project," a mining analyst said.
"Inco has put a very aggressive target out there of production in 1999. That's not very far away and I would still think it's a difficult objective to meet.
